title: A project group opens on its board, and waits for it
description:
Click a group whose page is served by one of its terminals — an Exos board, a wave page — and the page comes up by itself: a terminal the workspace file declares auto-run is started the first time the view finds its server down, instead of showing a dead page and a button after every restart.

A start is now patient. An Exos board refreshes from the hub before it serves, forty seconds on a good day and up to two minutes; the view used to give up at sixty and show "Server not responding" with the same Start button, whose click interrupted the refresh still running. It now stays on "Starting server…" with the seconds counting, and after a while offers the serving terminal ("Show terminal") and an explicit Restart — never a silent give-up. A start that cannot even spawn says why.

title: Edit documents and emails beside your agent
description:
Ask Claude Code or Codex to open a Markdown file, HTML file or email in your session. Your conversation stays on the left and the editor opens on the right; switching sessions brings both back together. Edits save automatically, with a visible conflict if the source changes elsewhere.

Emails have their own composer for recipients, the rendered body, signatures and attachments. Set a default signature file for future emails, choose a custom signature or leave it out for one draft. Existing drafts keep their staged signature and attachment copies. When ready, ask your agent to send the exact reviewed version through your configured Gmail connection.

title: A rendered page keeps its place — and the update card says what it brings
description:
Open an HTML file as a page, scroll into it, switch to another tab and come back: it used to start over — scroll at the top, the in-page tab you had picked closed, a chart's zoom reset. Only the tabs you were looking at were actually kept alive; the others were torn down and rebuilt on return. A dashboard or a workstream page now stays exactly where you left it, whether it is a file tab or a group's web view, the same way a terminal has always survived a switch.

The update card in the sidebar named a version and asked for a download. What was actually in that version, you found out afterwards — the release note ships inside the build it describes, so the copy running on your machine has never held the note for the version it is offering you. It now reads the release notes off GitHub as part of the update check and folds them under a **What's changed** line on the card; if you are several versions behind, every release between yours and the latest is there, newest first. The what's-new card underneath opens the same way, and stays a single headline until you ask.

And deleting a group now stops the quick-launch terminals it carried. It used to leave them running in tmux with no group to belong to, and the next launch adopted each one as a mystery tab. Delete and Ungroup ask first when a terminal is running, and say what they stop.

title: Codex usage and activity at a glance
description:
Codex now has a usage panel with your account's reported limits and reset times. The sidebar footer follows the selected agent: remaining capacity for Claude Code and Codex, or today's recorded tokens and cost for Pi. Click it to open that provider's usage panel.

The OpenAI icon now pulses blue while Codex works and clears when it is ready, needs your input, or exits. It works in background tabs and tmux sessions too. Relaunch existing Codex sessions to enable the indicator.

title: A group added to a .clave file stays one group
description:
Add a group to a workspace `.clave` file while Clave is running and it showed up once — then twice after the next launch, then three times, then four. The file was never wrong.

The pin the file watcher created for the new group carried no workspace stamp, and the next launch re-stamped it without clearing the copy it had left behind. Each restart hydrated both, stamped both, and saved one more.

A new pin now takes its workspace from the file it came from, a launch writes back every partition a pin moved out of, and the state file refuses to hold the same pin twice. A sidebar already showing duplicates is cleaned on the first launch of this build.

title: Your own shell starts your agents again
description:
Clave started every agent on macOS through `/bin/zsh`, whatever your login shell was. That looked like a no-op and was not.

macOS runs `path_helper` on login, and it *reorders* `PATH` — system directories first. A bash user's `.bash_profile` then puts their own entries back in front; their `.zshrc` never runs, because a `-l` zsh reads `.zprofile`, which they do not have. So an agent launched through zsh got the system binary where the same command in your own terminal got yours: a newer `git`, a `pyenv` shim, a `tar` you installed — shadowed, silently, inside every session.

Clave now keeps your shell for the launch when it is a POSIX one — `sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh`, `mksh`, `ash` — and diverts only the shells that cannot parse the wrapper it needs to run: `nu`, `fish` and the like. Nothing to set; if your login shell was already zsh, nothing changes.

title: Pull all pulls what you can see
description:
The ↓ in the git panel used to mean *go and check every repository in this folder, then pull whatever turns out to be behind*. On a folder of ninety repositories that is a minute of network time spent almost entirely on repositories with nothing to bring — and the button said “Fetching” the whole way through. One word, no repository, no count. Second 1 and second 90 looked the same, which is what a click that did nothing also looks like.

It is two controls now, and each one says what it does.

**↓ pulls the repositories showing a ↓ badge.** In parallel, in about a second, and nothing else — it never goes to a remote to look for more work. What the panel showed you is what it does. When nothing is badged the button is disabled and tells you why, instead of quietly sweeping ninety remotes to find out.

**Refresh is the sweep.** At the foot of the panel: it fetches every repository in the folder in parallel, and the badges it lands are what make the next ↓ complete. It is the slow one on purpose — better that the button which takes twenty seconds is the one labelled “refresh” than a pull that secretly sweeps before doing what you asked.

Both of them draw a **progress row** under the bar's controls: a track that fills as repositories finish, with `12/38` at its right end, and the summary of what happened held there for a few seconds afterwards. Magic sync uses the same row.

Underneath, every git call that talks to a remote now gives up after twenty seconds of silence and never prompts for credentials, so a single unreachable remote costs one repository instead of stalling everything behind it — and a fetch that fails now says so, where it used to leave the repository reported as “up to date”.

title: Keymaps you own — and Pi, and how your agents start
description:
Every shortcut in Clave is yours now. **Settings → Keymaps** lists all of them, records up to two bindings per action, and applies a valid draft to every open window the moment you press Save — nothing changes before that, and a configuration that conflicts with itself never replaces the one you had. There is raw JSON underneath if you would rather edit it that way, with import and export. The defaults are exactly the shortcuts you already know, plus one new thing: **⌘K** enters *command mode* — press it, then `C` within 300ms, and a Claude session starts. It is a ⌘ chord on purpose. Clave reads the keyboard before the terminal does, so a ⌃ master key would swallow tmux's own prefix and the shell's cursor keys inside every session. Unset it in Settings if you do not want command mode at all; the direct shortcuts keep working.

**How an agent starts is a setting too.** Settings → Agents holds named launch profiles: the command as an argument vector, plus any extra arguments, per agent family. If your `claude` lives behind a wrapper — `tokenops run -- env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY claude` — that is now a profile you pick, globally or for one workspace, and it shows up in the launcher's caret beside the agent it belongs to. Clave's own flags stay Clave's: a profile that tries to set `--session-id`, `--resume` or `--model` is refused rather than allowed to fight the app.

**Pi is a first-class agent**, beside Claude Code, Antigravity and Codex. ⌘⇧P launches one; its conversations are in History and resume from there; its tab carries the same working / done dots as a Claude tab, its provider, model and thinking level are profile defaults, and its token usage shows in the Usage pane. Two things Pi does not do, written down rather than discovered: it cannot call Clave's own tools, and its exchanges are not captured. Everything else — reading the tab, sending it a message, grouping it — works as usual.

And in the sidebar: **a new session lands at the top.** Where a launch landed used to depend on where you were standing — appended at the bottom, and quietly nested into whatever group held your selection — so the tab you had just asked for was the one you then had to go and find. It is the first row now, at the top level, whatever was selected. A session joins a group by being launched from that group's own **+**. A duplicate still appears directly under its original, and dragging a tab onto a group still drops it at the bottom.

Two smaller ones. The “Clave by Antasphere” mark stands clear of the traffic lights instead of crowding them, and stays put when you step into Settings or Extensions. And the sidebar's foot wears your own colour: that panel is made of your Antasphere field, and its controls were still lighting up in the app's grey, which over a coloured ground reads as dirt on the picture rather than as a control waking up. They take their hover from your palette's own signature hue now.

title: The side panel opens on the group — and copy copies the file
description:
The side panel's root was a fixed ladder: the focused tab's own folder first, its group's second, the workspace third. In practice that meant every tab in a group opened on whichever subfolder it happened to be launched in, and the one folder the group is actually about was a click away on every single tab. It is a preference now — Settings → General → Side panel → Default root — and it ships set to **the group**. It still falls through, so a tab outside any group still lands somewhere rather than on nothing, and the root chip on the panel still overrides it for one tab.

And the copy button on an open file now copies the file. It used to put the path on the clipboard — on the preview sheet, the file tab, and the diff tab alike — which is the one thing the file tree's right-click menu already offers twice. It hands over what you are looking at now: the document's text, unsaved edits included, or the patch as git printed it in a diff, with a check to say it happened.

Three smaller ones in the sidebar. The terminals button on a group header fits its count instead of squeezing the glyph, and a click on it opens the panel rather than toggling something hover has usually opened already. A group with terminals and no sessions no longer carries 6px of dead space under its title — the card is its header and nothing else — and with sessions, the space under the header reads as the seam between two rows. The agent caret in the launcher is a square button on the row's height, the same box as the folder picker beside it, instead of a 20px sliver between two proper buttons.

title: Every conversation on the Mac — and the message trail
description:
History (⌘⇧H) used to show the conversations Clave had run. It now opens on everything the Mac holds: the whole Claude transcript store — sessions from before Clave, `claude` runs from a plain terminal — plus the Codex CLI's sessions, each conversation placed in the right workspace by its own folder and counted literally in the footer: "285 claude sessions · 2 codex". Groups are filter chips over that universe now, not the universe itself. One search field does both depths: it narrows the rows as you type and searches inside the transcripts of everything in scope, through independent Human / Agent / Tools toggles — Human and Agent on by default — and Codex transcripts answer the same toggles. Codex rows are titled by their first message; resume stays a click away for Claude conversations, exactly as before. The panel itself got quieter: one row of controls, the panel family's own search field and buttons, and about 80 phantom "conversations" — Clave's own tab-title helper calls — recognized and gone for good.

And every Claude tab now answers "what was this about?" without scrolling: a small box floats at the top of the terminal carrying the conversation's human messages — the newest by default, chevrons to walk back, and under each message the first line of the agent's final answer for that turn. Hovering the title reveals the panel: the surrounding turns with their times, the current one reading whole. Clicking a message scrolls the terminal to that point in the discussion. The trail reads the live transcript itself, so it follows the conversation as it grows and survives restarts and /clear; the speech-bubble button in the tab's header hides it everywhere at once.

Smaller: folders in the file tree open and close instantly again (the unfold animation put a wait in front of a click you make dozens of times a minute), and a gitignored file is drawn grey from the first frame instead of flashing black.

title: The chrome, squared up — and a softer dark
description:
A fourth theme: Charcoal. The default dark is off-black, which reads as a hole cut out of the screen; Charcoal is the same architecture painted on warm charcoal instead — one hue held at low chroma through the whole ramp so the greys are ash rather than slate, bigger steps between the surfaces because a lifted ground stops letting a 1px border do the separating, and nothing in it pure black, down to the modal scrim, the overlay shadows and the terminal's own ANSI black. It brings its own terminal palette and source-code highlighting rather than borrowing the light theme's. Settings › Appearance; nothing changes for anyone who does not pick it.

Every button in the chrome is one size. The toolbar had two on the same row — the buttons your workspace declares were 28px while the sidebar toggle, the file search and the file-tree toggle beside them were 24 — and that is why the two panel toggles sat with more air above them than beside them: a smaller button cannot reach the space a bigger one does. Underneath it the size classes were paddings rather than boxes, so a button came out as whatever glyph it happened to hold; one terminal header carried a save, a plan and a close at three different sizes. They are fixed squares now, the toolbar is uniformly the larger one, and a terminal header's buttons match each other for the first time. The side panel's path bar joins its own Files/Git tabs at that size too.

And the corners answer the boxes they sit in. Every control inside one of the app's panels — the launcher's buttons, the group switcher's chips and its search field, the panel tabs, the panel's icon buttons — was a pixel squarer than the panel around it. A panel insets its contents by 3px, so its 10px corner wants a 7px one inside it; they had 6. Visible on every hover fill in the app once you have seen it.

In the file tree, the disclosure chevrons step back. They wore exactly the ink of the folder icon and the name beside them — a third mark competing with two, hardest in light mode — and take 60% of it now, in every theme. Opening a folder no longer inserts its children between one frame and the next either: the rows grow from nothing over a sixth of a second, so the list below glides instead of jumping. Reduced motion switches it off.

The Git tab's controls stay inside the panel. Six of them never fitted the panel's default width and the bar was told not to wrap, so the last two ran off its edge and out of the window, where nothing could click them. The bar now splits in two: everything naming the repo takes the slack on its line and truncates inside itself, and the controls move to a second line whole.

title: History: a group’s past sessions, back with one click
description:
Right-click a group and pick History (or press ⌘⇧H for everything): every Claude conversation that lived in that group, open or long closed, one row each — Claude Code’s own title for the session, the last thing you said in it and when, sorted by that last message. Click a row and the conversation comes back as a tab in the group with its whole context; ⌥-click skips permissions; a live one is simply focused. Clave never kept the link between a closed tab and its group before — the record went with the tab — so it now writes its own small ledger the moment a session is placed or moved, whatever moved it: a drag, ⌘G, an agent. A group relaunched from its pin keeps its history, matched by name as well as by id, and a transcript Claude Code has cleaned up stays listed, greyed. The field filters instantly on titles, last messages, folders and group names; switch it to Human, Agent or Tools and it searches inside the transcripts of the rows on screen — what you typed, what the agent answered, or the tools it called — with the matching excerpt under each row. Also fixed on the way: after a /clear the tab kept the old transcript’s id, so Resume and a restart reopened the conversation you had just cleared.

The side panel chooses its root. The file tree and the git panel only ever knew the focused tab’s folder — with no tab focused the panel drew nothing, and a tab deep in one repo had no way to look at the workspace around it. The path bar now opens with a root chip, W, G or S, whose menu offers the workspace root, the group’s folder and the session’s own, each greyed when there is nothing on that rung, with the folder picker underneath since any folder is a root too. The default is a ladder: the session’s folder when there is one, else its group’s, else the workspace — so an empty window shows the workspace’s tree and repos instead of a blank panel — and every session keeps what you picked for it until you pick again.

title: Groups come back whole, and open where they should
description:
Quit Clave with a group running and it comes back as itself. The record a session leaves behind never said what the session was FOR, and every spawn writes one — so a group's dev server, a session view's serving process and a toolbar button's server all left a record indistinguishable from a tab's, and the restore adopted each as a tab. You got mystery rows beside your groups, while the thing that owned them showed "not running" and its start button spawned a second server on the same port. Records now carry what they are attached to, and the restore sorts them before adopting any: a hidden half re-links to its owner instead of becoming a row, a live toolbar terminal is parked for its button to pick up again, and a hidden half that died is let go rather than resurrected as a bare shell in the same folder. A group whose tabs did not come back also survives now if one of its terminals did — it used to be pruned, which un-nested the terminal that had come back.

A group's `+` opens where the group's own tab opened. Project groups are declared to start at the workspace root, with the whole tree in reach, while the group's folder stays the small project directory its brief points at. The `+` was reading only the second half of that, so the second tab in a group sat a directory or more deep from the first — same group, same button, same brief, somewhere else, and nothing on screen said so. It reproduces the declared session whole now, brief and directory both. Groups already running pick this up from the workspace file they came from, so you do not need to relaunch anything.

The group header reads `+` first, then the terminals. The two controls swapped places and the count moved in front of the icon it counts, so the row ends on `+ 3 ⌨` rather than `⌨ 3 +`. The terminals panel opens to the right of the sidebar now instead of downwards into it: it lists each terminal's command and folder, which is wider than the sidebar and taller than the rows underneath, so opening downwards covered the very groups you were choosing between. It opens level with the group's own row and clears the sidebar's edge at whatever width you have dragged it to.

Every popover is one of the sidebar's boxes now, lifted off the page. The workspace switcher, the agent menu, every context menu, the file preview, the diff and journey sheets, the file palette, the commit bar's pull menu and the side panel's folder menu all sat on a surface one shade off the boxes they open from — the hover colour of their own rows, in fact — and several still wore corners, borders and shadows of their own. One surface, one radius, one shadow for menus and a heavier one for the document-sized sheets, and the row you are currently on inside takes the sidebar's selected fill.

The mark in the top-left corner is a size up and a weight up, and it says who makes the thing: "by Antasphere" beside it, a step smaller and a weight lighter, on the same baseline. Click the name and the house's site opens. In fullscreen it goes all the way to the left — there are no traffic lights to keep clear of there, so the 84px the mark was holding for them was a hole, and it now sits at 16px, where the first button would have been. The toolbar does the same with the sidebar closed, since that is when it is the toolbar running under those buttons. Drag the sidebar narrow enough and the attribution steps aside rather than being clipped mid-letter.

Smaller things: the vertical indent guides are gone from the Files tab — one hairline per level down every row is a lot of repeated ink to say what the indentation and the chevrons already say, and the horizontal rules between rows are what you actually read a block by. And the side panel's path box starts on the content card's top edge instead of four pixels above it.

title: The side panel, squared up
description:
The panel on the right had its controls spread across rows by accident rather than by subject. The bar on top carried the tabs plus the folder picker, collapse-all and a help button; it carries the tabs now and nothing else, in a box the width of Files and Git rather than a full-width frame with two buttons adrift in it. Everything about where the panel is pointed moved down and joined the path, which is a box of its own instead of a bare line of text: the folder picker opens it, the path names it and drops its parents, the back arrow and the way home flank it, and collapse-all closes what it opened. The help button left the panel's corner entirely — ⌘? still opens help.

The Files tab is ruled like the Git tab. The same hairline sits between rows at the depth of the row below it, so opening a folder shows you where its contents begin and end instead of a run of names with nothing between them. Every row takes one but the first, a folder and the first thing inside it included — that pairing was the last one held back, and holding it back read as ruling that gives out halfway down the panel.

It also reads at the Git tab's size. The file tree ran on a tighter gutter and a tighter indent than the tree beside it, so the same names came out as a denser, smaller list rather than as the same tree showing different things. One gutter, one indent, one chevron across both, and the indent guides run down the middle of their level's chevron column.

At the other edge of the window, the sidebar's list now ends on a seam at both ends. The one under the group switcher said the cards scroll behind the chrome above them; at the bottom the list just ran out into the foot panel. It closes on the same hairline with the same 4px, mirrored, and only while the list actually overflows — with nothing scrolling under the foot there is no edge for a seam to be.

title: Both edges of the window, reworked
description:
The sidebar is reworked end to end, and the side panel opposite it now speaks the same language.

Dragging a session works the way the hand expects. A drag carries the row under the cursor and nothing else — clicking a group header selects every row in it, so dragging any one row used to empty the whole group into the drop target and delete it. Every row offers a top and a bottom half, so the first and last position of another group can be aimed at; from inside, a group's header means "first position"; and a row's own place always means "stay", so changing your mind mid-drag no longer moves the row out. Rows of a collapsed group stop catching drops meant for the group underneath. The drop line itself is drawn over the seam between rows and takes no space at all — it used to be a slot inserted into the list, so every time it moved the rows lurched under a cursor that had not moved. When the line snaps to a new row the trackpad gives the same quiet tick Finder uses, so the hand feels the target change without the eye leaving what it is dragging.

A group header no longer lays every terminal's icon out in a row that ran off the sidebar past a handful, truncating the group's name first. It carries one terminals button showing how many are attached, lit in a running terminal's colour, which opens a panel listing each one with its icon, command, folder and a running dot — click to start or focus, right-click to edit, New terminal at the foot.

Typing in the group switcher now shows you what Enter will do: the first chip left standing takes the state hovering it gives, so the key you are about to press has a visible target instead of being a guess you confirm by pressing it. Cmd+F reaches the field again — the shortcut had been aiming at an attribute the rebuilt field no longer carried, so it opened the sidebar and focused nothing. The chip row collapses when it holds no chips instead of keeping a line open to announce that the panel is empty. And the list below no longer dies against the switcher: the cards scroll behind it, and with nothing between them they slid up into its bottom border, which made the panel read as the first row of the list rather than as the chrome the list runs under. There is now the same 4px that holds the launcher and the switcher apart, closed by a hairline.

At the bottom, three rows of different shapes — a feedback card, a work tracker, a bare user button — become one panel, cut from the same cloth as the launcher and the switcher above, so the list is bracketed by chrome at both ends instead of trailing off. Its ground is the Antasphere generative field, and your avatar is that field at full strength with the glyph knocked out of it; Settings offers a painted swatch per palette and a redraw, because no hex describes a field. The second line stops counting minutes worked and starts answering "can I keep going": your tightest usage window as percent left, with a meter that drains. Nothing names a cap — which ones an account has is the service's business — so it takes whatever came back and shows whichever is closest to stopping you.

Files and Git are under one chrome now. The bar on top carries what belongs to both tabs — the folder the panel points at, collapse-all, help — instead of one copy per tab, and under it each tab brings its own: the search field for Files, the git controls for Git. The repo tree draws its rules at the head of a block, at the depth of the row that opens it, so a folder holding repos is ruled between its folders rather than under every repo inside them. And "N repos — live updates paused" stopped being a warning strip across the top of the list you came to read: a big tree is a fact about the folder, not a fault, so it is a folded footnote at the foot of the panel with the current limit, a refresh, and one button that opens the setting.

Inside the Git tab, orange leaves the two places it least belonged. A file you changed and a commit waiting on the remote are the normal life of a repo, and painting both as warnings meant a healthy repo showed a wall of them. Modified takes the app's own accent, incoming a plain informational blue, and green, red and blue keep their conventional meanings. Orange survives on exactly one row — a file that an incoming change and your working tree both touch — so the one real heads-up reads. A repo's files sit on the same row height as the file tree above them, the blocks inside a repo have air between them, and the vertical indent guides came down to about a third of their old weight: repeated once per level on every row, at a border's strength they read as a table's gridlines rather than as a guide.

title: Several windows — the whole app, as many times as you like
description:
Clave can run in several windows at once. A window is the app once more: put it on whatever workspace you want — the same one as another window included — and work there. File › New Window (⌘⇧N) opens one on the workspace you are looking at, and every workspace row in the toolbar switcher has an Open in new window action. Tabs and groups live in the window you opened them in, and that is all a window means: your sidebar in each window is its own, and every window comes back at the next launch on its workspace, at its size and place, with its groups and sessions.

Right-click a tab or a group for Move to window… — the tab keeps its id and its scrollback (tmux-backed sessions only; a plain terminal stays where it is). Closing a window kills nothing: its tabs and groups land in the first window. Switching a window's workspace touches nothing else.

Agents got the same reach: clave_open_session, clave_create_group, clave_launch_group and friends take a window to land in, clave_open_window opens one, clave_move_session moves a tab across windows, and clave_list reports the windows and which one holds each tab.

For anyone running Clave's own test suite: test instances no longer appear on screen at all.

title: One surface language, from the sidebar to the menus
description:
The sidebar's top controls are a panel now, cut from the same cloth as the toolbar and the terminal cards — same border, same surface, same height, and a top edge that lines up exactly with the first card beside it. The buttons inside dropped their pill fills: the panel already frames them, so the row reads as hairlines and hover states instead of loose chips on a bare field.

Under it, a new group switcher. It lists the groups you have running, with All to come back to everything, and a search field that widens it to every group the workspace knows about — including the ones declared in .clave or auto-discovered from your tree that are not running yet. A group the search finds but that is not started appears under the results as a closed card with a Start button, so reaching a group you have not opened no longer means leaving the sidebar for the picker dialog. Chips wrap instead of scrolling sideways.

The list itself has room to breathe: taller rows, larger icons, more padding. Groups behave properly too — hovering a group's header now lights the whole group in its own colour, and every control inside a coloured group takes that colour instead of a grey that never belonged there. A group's terminal icons stay readable when the group is not the one you are looking at, which is exactly when you need to see which of them is running.

The surfaces that float over the app caught up in the same release. Menus, popovers, tooltips and dialogs share one language: the panel's radius and border, quiet inset rows, and a single scrim in place of the three different ones that were in use. They also animate — the enter and exit classes they relied on came from a plugin that was never installed, so every menu used to teleport. The terminal grid keeps zero animation on purpose: appearing instantly is the point. If you have reduced motion switched on, every entrance collapses to a fast fade.

title: Software Update, where you can actually reach it
description:
Clave now has a Software Update pane in Settings and a Check for Updates… item in the menu bar — the two places a Mac app is supposed to keep them. The pane shows the version you are running, whether a newer one exists, when Clave last looked, and a Download & Install button with live progress.

This fixes a real way of getting stuck. The update notice used to be a banner pushed to the sidebar once, five seconds after launch and then every half hour. If you missed it, dismissed it, or the check quietly failed, nothing on screen would admit an update existed and there was no way to ask — which, since auto-update is how Clave ships, meant no way to upgrade. The app now holds that state and hands it over whenever the window asks, so the answer survives a restart.

When an update will not install, the pane stops being a dead end: a link to install the release by hand, and a link to the updater log that says why it failed. A download that dies mid-transfer also retries itself once before bothering you.

title: Views you declare, workspaces in the toolbar
description:
A group's page can now be declared in its .clave file rather than set by hand: a quick-launch terminal marked "groupView": true binds its server as the group's web view at launch, and a group-level "view" names a page that needs no process at all. Single sessions get the same thing without a group — an agent can attach a live dashboard to its own tab, which persists across restarts and starts again in one click. An untrusted .clave file never renders a page.

The workspace switcher moved to the toolbar: click the workspace name to see every workspace on this machine and switch with one click, and add one straight from the folder picker instead of a detour through Settings. The sidebar's pill row is gone.

In the git panel the change count is now a button like the sync arrows — click it to fold the local file list away and leave just what a pull or push would carry. Those sections get a spelled-out Pull (rebase) and Push back in their headers, a clean repo says so inside a contained field, and every list scrolls a little past its last row instead of ending flush.

Plus a pass over the things that shifted under you: tree rows no longer resize when a badge appears, dividers follow the tree's indentation, panels lost their drop shadow, and several buttons that were a few pixels off now line up.

title: A new git panel, a new launcher, less chrome
description:
The git panel is now your real folder tree: repos sit where they live on disk, single-child chains merge into one row, and folders fold with rolled-up change counts. The ↓ and ↑ badges are buttons — they unfold Incoming and Outgoing sections listing every file a pull will bring or a push will send, with a ⚠ on files you also changed locally. The commit bar is tucked behind the pencil icon.

Starting a session no longer asks where: the launcher is split into a terminal button and an agent button that remembers the agent you last used in that workspace, opens at the workspace root, and keeps a folder button for anywhere else. Groups carry their own prompt, so a group's + starts a session already briefed. And the launcher stays pinned instead of scrolling away.

Groups can also open as live pages — attach a dev server, a dashboard or an HTML file and clicking the group renders it instead of the terminals. HTML files render in their own tabs too, with a Rendered ⇄ Source toggle. Gone, because nobody used them: the Extensions entry and the toolbar's detected-URL tags. Terminals now reach the edges of their panes.

title: Server buttons in the toolbar
description: Give a quick-launch terminal a serverUrl and its button becomes a service switch: one click starts the server if needed and opens it in your browser, with a live status dot showing up, starting, or down.

title: Edit markdown right on the page
description: Page mode is now a Notion-style writing surface — click anywhere and type. Headings, lists and code blocks convert as you write, checkboxes toggle with a click, and ⌘S saves clean markdown back to the file.

title: Markdown opens as a page
description: Markdown files now render as a document-style page by default — a centered reading column with real typography, frontmatter hidden and its title on top. The compact preview and the source editor stay one click away via the new Page / Preview / Source switcher.

title: Agents can show you files and notify you
description: Agents in your tabs gained two new tools: clave_open_file opens a document they produced as a file tab for you to read or edit, and clave_notify sends a native notification when long-running work finishes in a tab you are not looking at — click it to jump straight there.

title: Spot Clave in Mission Control
description: When you open macOS Mission Control or App Exposé, Clave now covers its window with a blurred overlay and a large Clave mark, so you can pick it out instantly among the thumbnails. No extra permissions needed — toggle it under Settings → Appearance.

title: Antigravity CLI replaces Gemini CLI
description: Google retired the standalone Gemini CLI and folded it into the new Antigravity CLI. Cmd+I and the New session menu now launch the Antigravity CLI (the agy binary) with its brand mark. Your existing Gemini sessions, pinned groups, and .clave files keep working and reopen as Antigravity automatically.

title: Install plugins from Extensions
description: The Extensions view is no longer read-only — you can now manage plugins right inside Clave. Open a marketplace to install any plugin it offers or remove the marketplace, open an installed plugin to enable, disable, or uninstall it, and use Add marketplace to register a new one from a GitHub repo, git URL, or local path. Disabled plugins are flagged so you can tell them apart. Changes apply the next time you start a Claude session.

title: Trusted workspace folders
description: Adding a workspace folder now trusts it as a root, so every .clave file inside it opens without re-prompting — no more repeated warning dialogs when you run many workspaces or when a file gets rewritten. A new Trusted workspace folders card in Settings lists your trusted roots and lets you revoke any of them. Files opened from outside a trusted folder still ask for confirmation.

title: Browse your installed Extensions
description: A new Extensions view (under New Session in the sidebar) shows everything installed for a Claude Code profile. Browse your marketplaces as cards, drill into one to see its plugins, then open a plugin to see its skills, agents, commands, and MCP servers. A dedicated MCP Servers tab lists every server across all sources, and when you run multiple Claude accounts a profile dropdown scopes the whole view.

title: Anonymous usage ping
description: Clave now sends one anonymous ping a day — a random ID, the app version, and your platform, nothing else — so we know how many people use it. The exact payload is documented in the README, and a new Privacy section in Settings → General lets you turn it off with one click.

title: A redesigned Settings page
description: Settings is now a full page with its own sidebar — General, Appearance, and Usage — replacing the footer popup. Options are grouped into clean cards with slim controls, and the sidebar footer is a compact row whose gear takes you straight to Settings.

title: Agents can now drive Clave
description: A Claude session can open new agent tabs with an initial prompt and launch your pinned workspace groups through a built-in MCP server — so a coordinating agent can set up and hand off work across tabs. Agents can also request a secret without it ever showing in the chat: you review the action in the toolbar and paste the value into a masked field, scoped to that one action.

title: Git panel stays current in large folders
description: When a folder has many repositories, the Git panel pauses live polling — but it no longer goes stale silently. It now refreshes automatically when an agent finishes a turn or the window regains focus, shows the last update time with a refresh spinner, and a new Git section in Settings lets you change the pause threshold or turn pausing off entirely.

title: Run multiple Claude accounts side by side
description: Define Claude Code accounts in Settings, each pointing at its own config directory. With more than one, a picker appears when you start a Claude session and each session's header shows which account it's running under — so a work and a personal account can run in parallel without touching environment variables.

title: Sessions that survive quitting
description: Sessions now run inside tmux, so your agents keep going after you quit Clave, survive crashes, and reattach automatically next launch — reachable from any terminal via `tmux -L clave attach`. On by default when tmux is installed; toggle it in Settings → Sessions.

title: Live status on session tabs
description: Claude Code tabs now show their status at a glance: the icon pulses blue while working, an amber dot means Claude is waiting on your input, and a green dot flags a session that finished while you were away. Driven by Claude Code's own lifecycle signals, so it's accurate, not guessed.

title: Claude Agents sessions
description: Launch a `claude agents` session from the New session menu or with ⌘⇧A. A faint trailing glyph in the sidebar tells Claude Agents and skip-permissions sessions apart from plain Claude Code.

title: Redesigned agent conversations
description: The remote agent chat has a fresh look — your messages in clean rounded bubbles, agent replies as easy-to-read flowing text, and a refined composer with a circular send button.

title: Provider logos in the sidebar
description: Sessions now show their provider's real logo — Claude Code, Gemini, and Codex each display their brand mark in the sidebar, so you can tell them apart at a glance.

title: Edit files right in Clave
description: Files now open syntax-highlighted and instantly editable — just click into the code, type, and press ⌘S to save. Highlighting follows your theme, and markdown opens rendered with a Source toggle.

title: Templates launcher
description: Your .clave session templates now open from a folder-plus icon next to the Sessions header, in a searchable popover — so a long list of templates no longer crowds your sessions.

title: Codex CLI sessions
description: Launch OpenAI's Codex CLI from the New session menu or with Cmd+U, just like Claude Code and Gemini CLI.

title: Sidebar selection focus
description: Selecting a session, group, or file tab now fades the unselected rows so your active selection stands out at a glance.

title: Redesigned sidebar
description: A cleaner sidebar: New session and Queue as top tabs, your sessions under one Sessions header with pinned groups inline, consistent spacing and alignment from shared design tokens, and slightly less round corners across the app.

title: Publish Branch from the Git panel
description: Committing on a brand-new local branch now surfaces a Publish Branch button in the Git panel — it pushes the branch to origin with upstream tracking so your commits don't sit there invisibly.

title: Undo in the sidebar
description: Press Cmd+Z to undo the last sidebar action — disbanding a group, dragging a session, renaming, or recoloring. Up to 50 steps are remembered.

title: Windows Support
description: Clave now ships a Windows installer alongside every macOS release — Windows users can download a `.exe` setup directly from GitHub Releases

title: Model Pill
description: See the active Claude model at a glance in the terminal header — click for a popover with reasoning effort, thinking, fast mode, context window, and live session cost. Everything stays up to date via Claude Code's statusLine hook

title: Context Inventory
description: See what Claude Code loads into context per session — CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, MCP, hooks — with a live percentage badge, category breakdown, and estimated token cost

title: Open Git Diffs as Tabs
description: Double-click any changed file to preview, then open the diff as a persistent document tab — with live stage/unstage and right-click access from the git tree

title: Daily Cost Tracking
description: See exactly how much you spend per day, week, or month with the new cost bar chart on the Usage page

title: Activity Heatmap
description: Your Usage page now shows a full year of activity as a GitHub-style contribution heatmap

title: Smarter Work Tracker
description: Accurate wall-clock time tracking with concurrent session support, now integrated into the sidebar footer

title: Design System & Chat History
description: Unified design tokens across the app, and a new chat bubble layout for browsing conversation history

title: Work Tracker
description: Track your daily coding sessions, build streaks, and visualize weekly trends right from the sidebar
